data: Kuiper Belt Object · Cold-classical · Contact binary

The most distant body ever visited by a spacecraft — 4.1 billion km from the Sun when New Horizons flew within 3,500 km on New Year's Day 2019. Its two lobes (Wenu and Weeyo) gently merged at the dawn of the solar system and have stayed merged for 4.5 billion years at ~40 K.

Cold-classical Kuiper Belt object — the most distant body ever visited by a spacecraft (4.1 billion km from the Sun at encounter). A 36 × 20 × 10 km contact binary nicknamed 'the snowman', formed when two lobes (Wenu and Weeyo) gently merged in the early solar system. New Horizons flew within 3,500 km on 2019-01-01, returning images of a deep-red, primordial KBO surface preserved at ~40 K since accretion.
New Horizons — NASA, 1 January 2019 flyby (most distant body ever visited at the time)
486958 Arrokoth (visited by New Horizons in 2019) is the most distant solar-system object ever explored — a primordial Kuiper-belt contact binary that has likely never been warmed by the Sun.
Arrokoth orbits at 44.6 AU — classical Kuiper Belt, beyond Pluto, in a region where bodies have been mostly undisturbed since the early solar system.
A disc of icy bodies beyond Neptune — predicted in 1951, confirmed in 1992, and the source of every short-period comet that flies past Earth.
Half the longest diameter of the orbit ellipse — and the single number that sets the orbital period.
